items.prose: A waiting time $X$, in minutes, has density $f(x) = \tfrac13 e^{-x/3}$ for $x \ge 0$.
items.question: Write $P(X > x)$ for $x \ge 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the density from $x$ to infinity.

byKey.cdf: That is $P(X \le x)$, the area to the left.
byKey.density: That is the density itself, a height. The tail is an area.

explain.text: $\int_x^\infty \tfrac13 e^{-s/3}\,ds = \left[-e^{-s/3}\right]_x^\infty = e^{-x/3}$. This is the exponential with rate $\tfrac13$ a minute, mean 3 minutes.

items.prose: Losses $X$ above £1m, in £m, have density $f(x) = \tfrac{3}{x^4}$ for $x \ge 1$.
items.question: What is $P(X > 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $3x^{-4}$ from 2 to infinity.

byKey.height: 0.1875 is $f(2)$, a height. Integrate for the area.

explain.text: An antiderivative of $3x^{-4}$ is $-x^{-3}$. From 2 to infinity that gives $0 + 2^{-3} = 0.125$. One loss in 8 above £1m exceeds £2m.

items.title: The exponential mean
items.prose: Derive $E[T] = \tfrac{1}{\lambda}$ for the exponential density $\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$, $t \ge 0$.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $E[T] = \int_0^\infty t\,\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt$, the mean of a density
$= \left[-t e^{-\lambda t}\right]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,dt$, by parts with $u = t$ and $v = -e^{-\lambda t}$
$= 0 + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,dt$, since $t e^{-\lambda t}$ is 0 at $t = 0$ and tends to 0 as $t \to \infty$

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate by parts before dealing with the boundary term.

byKey.parts: Integration by parts acts on the integral, so the definition comes first.
byKey.bound: The boundary term appears only after integrating by parts.
byKey.eval: The last integral can be evaluated only once the boundary term is gone.

explain.text: With $u = t$ and $dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt$, the boundary term vanishes because $e^{-\lambda t}$ beats $t$. The remaining area is $\tfrac1\lambda$. At 2 trades a minute that is the 30-second mean gap.

items.prose: A fund's annual return $X$, in %, is normal. It beats 25% one year in 20, and loses more than 5% one year in 10.
items.question: What is the sd of $X$, in percentage points? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write one equation per quantile, then subtract them.

byKey.two-sided: You used 1.96 for the 5% tail. One tail of 5% needs 1.645.
byKey.same-z: You used 1.645 for both tails. The 10% tail needs $\Phi^{-1}(0.1) = -1.2816$.

explain.text: $P(X > 25) = 0.05$ gives $\mu + 1.645\sigma = 25$, and $P(X < -5) = 0.1$ gives $\mu - 1.2816\sigma = -5$. Subtracting, $2.9265\sigma = 30$, so $\sigma \approx 10.25$ and $\mu \approx 8.14$.

items.prose: A bond's prices imply a 5-year survival probability of 0.85 for its issuer, under a constant hazard rate.
items.question: What is the hazard rate, in % a year? Give 2 decimal places.

widget.label: Hazard rate in percent a year

byKey.linear: You spread the 15% default chance evenly over 5 years. Survival decays as $e^{-5\lambda}$, so take logs.
byKey.annual: $1 - 0.85^{1/5}$ treats default as a once-a-year draw. A constant hazard acts continuously.

explain.text: Taking logs, $-5\lambda = \ln 0.85 \approx -0.1625$, so $\lambda \approx 0.0325$, 3.25% a year. Credit desks back out hazard rates from prices exactly like this.

items.prose: A £100 share has drift $m = 5\%$ and volatility $\sigma = 20\%$ a year, in the lognormal model.
items.question: What is $P(90 < S_1 < 110)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take logs of both ends, then standardise with log drift 0.03 and sd 0.2.

byKey.normal: You put a normal on $S_1$ itself. Standardise $\ln S_1$ instead.
byKey.no-drag: You used 0.05 as the log drift. Subtract $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = 0.02$.

items.prose: You hold £1m of the share above ($m = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$, lognormal). The 1-year 99% VaR is the loss exceeded with chance 1%. Use $\Phi(-2.326) = 0.01$.
items.question: What is the 1-year 99% VaR, in pounds?

feedback.correct: The 1% price is $e^{0.03 - 0.4652} \approx 0.6471$ of today's, so the VaR is about £352,900.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the 1% quantile of $\ln(S_1/S_0)$, exponentiate, then compute the loss.

byKey.normal-ret: You treated the simple return as normal, $0.05 - 2.326 \times 0.2$. In this model the log return is normal.
byKey.no-drag: You used 0.05 as the log drift. The log drifts at $0.05 - 0.02 = 0.03$.
byKey.no-mean: You left out the log drift of 0.03. It moves the quantile up slightly.

explain.text: The 1% quantile of $\ln(S_1/S_0)$ is $0.03 - 2.326 \times 0.2 = -0.4352$. So the 1% price ratio is $e^{-0.4352} \approx 0.6471$, a loss of about £352,900. A normal on simple returns says £415,200, because it lets prices go below zero.

items.title: The exponential, start to finish
items.prompt:
Let $T$ have density $f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \ge 0$ (and 0 for $t < 0$), with $\lambda > 0$.

(a) Show that $f$ is a density, and find the CDF $F(t)$ and the survival function $P(T > t)$.

(b) Find the median of $T$, and say why it is below the mean $\tfrac1\lambda$.

(c) Prove that $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$ for $s, t \ge 0$.

(d) An issuer defaults at a constant hazard rate of 3% a year. Find its 10-year survival probability, and the chance it defaults in years 6 to 10 given that it survives the first 5.

(e) A colleague says the issuer is a safer credit after surviving 5 years. Comment, saying what the model assumes and when that assumption fails.
items.model:
**(a)** For $t \ge 0$, $f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t} > 0$, and $f = 0$ below 0, so $f \ge 0$ everywhere. Its total area is an improper integral:

$$\int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda t}\,dt = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left[-e^{-\lambda t}\right]_0^b = \lim_{b \to \infty}\left(1 - e^{-\lambda b}\right) = 1.$$

So $f$ is a density. For $t \ge 0$ the CDF is the running area, $F(t) = \int_0^t \lambda e^{-\lambda s}\,ds = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$ (and $F(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$). The survival function is $P(T > t) = 1 - F(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.

**(b)** The median $t_m$ solves $P(T > t_m) = \tfrac12$: $e^{-\lambda t_m} = \tfrac12$, so $t_m = \tfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda} \approx \tfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$. This is below the mean $\tfrac1\lambda$. The density is highest at 0 and has a long right tail: most waits are short, but rare long waits pull the mean up, while the median ignores how far out they lie. Indeed $P(T > \tfrac1\lambda) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368 < \tfrac12$.

**(c)** By the definition of conditional probability,

$$P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = \frac{P(T > s + t \text{ and } T > s)}{P(T > s)}.$$

Since $t \ge 0$, the event $T > s + t$ already implies $T > s$, so the numerator is $P(T > s + t)$. Using (a),

$$\frac{e^{-\lambda(s + t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(T > t).$$

**(d)** With $\lambda = 0.03$, the 10-year survival is $P(T > 10) = e^{-0.3} \approx 0.7408$. Given survival to year 5, the chance of default in years 6 to 10 is

$$P(T \le 10 \mid T > 5) = 1 - P(T > 10 \mid T > 5) = 1 - e^{-0.03 \times 5} = 1 - e^{-0.15} \approx 0.1393,$$

using (c). Check: $1 - \tfrac{e^{-0.3}}{e^{-0.15}} = 1 - e^{-0.15}$, the same.

**(e)** Under a constant hazard the colleague is wrong. By (c) the issuer that has survived 5 years faces exactly the same default distribution as a new one: a 13.9% chance of default over the next 5 years, the same as over the first 5. Survival carries no information about the future in this model. The assumption is that the hazard rate does not change. It fails when the issuer's credit quality moves: a firm that pays down debt may become safer, while one in decline or facing a large bond maturity becomes riskier. Market hazard rates implied from bond or CDS prices therefore vary with the horizon and over time.

rubric.text: (a) Shows $f \ge 0$ and evaluates the improper integral to 1, with the limit.
(a) Gives $F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \ge 0$ and $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.
(b) Solves $e^{-\lambda t} = \tfrac12$ to get the median $\tfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.
(b) Explains the median is below the mean through the long right tail (or $P(T > \tfrac1\lambda) = e^{-1} < \tfrac12$).
(c) Writes the conditional probability as a ratio by its definition.
(c) Justifies that $\{T > s + t\} \cap \{T > s\} = \{T > s + t\}$.
(c) Substitutes the survival function and cancels $e^{-\lambda s}$.
(d) Gets $1 - e^{-0.15} \approx 0.1393$ for default in years 6 to 10 given survival to 5.
(e) States the model gives no gain in safety and names the constant-hazard assumption and a way it fails.
